references.text: Hosea uses similar language to describe Israel's sin as something unheard of and shocking, requiring reflection and a response from the people.
The reference to when the children of Israel came up out of Egypt is used as a starting point to measure the passage of time and historical events.
Saul sends pieces of oxen to all the tribes of Israel with a similar message calling the people to action, echoing the Levite's act involving his concubine.
The sin of Sodom is used as a comparison with the wickedness in Gibeah, where sexual immorality and violence against guests were central elements.
Hosea refers directly to the days of Gibeah as an example of deep corruption in Israel.
The prophet Hosea looks back on the sin at Gibeah as a historical low point for Israel's moral condition.
